episodes.214240: On the 26th late evening, an unstable atmospheric environment combined with a weak surface boundary to trigger localized cluster thunderstorm development across southwestern Indiana. High precipitable water values and moderate deep-layer shear supported brief convective intensification as the activity tracked southeastward through the region.||The severe thunderstorms produced localized straight-line wind gusts estimated near 58 mph across portions of Knox County around 9:49 PM EST. These severe winds resulted in isolated damage across the area, primarily consisting of downed trees and broken limbs blocking local roadways before the convective activity diminished later into the night.
episodes.214246: During the 27th afternoon and evening, a warm unstable air mass interacting with an upper wave and associated surface boundary developed scattered severe thunderstorms across central Indiana. Convection initiated around 15:27 EST over northern portions of central Indiana and overspread locations further south before diminishing during the evening hours.||Severe thunderstorm wind gusts were the primary hazard, with peak gusts estimated and measured between 58 mph and 60 mph. Official surface observations included a 58 mph gust recorded by the Muncie ASOS (KMIE) in Delaware County and a 59 mph gust at the Indianapolis ASOS (KIND) in Marion County. Wind damage was scattered across most eastern counties and a couple western zones, with numerous downed trees and powerlines, snapped utility poles and localized structural damage. Hail up to 1.25 inches in diameter was reported in Marion and Warren county, with broken windows in Warren county from wind-driven hail.||Additionally, torrential rainfall of 1.20-2.00 inches in approximately 30 minutes resulted in localized flash flooding in Marion County between 17:00 and 21:00 EST. Rapid runoff inundated low-lying roadways, stranded or partially submerged multiple vehicles in high water, and caused localized yard and basement flooding.
episodes.214260: A line of thunderstorms moved south through Middle Tennessee during the late evening hours of July 26, 2026, through the early morning hours of July 27, 2026. Despite a highly unstable atmosphere, these thunderstorms weakened as they tracked through Middle Tennessee and an outflow boundary raced ahead. This outflow boundary was primarily the cause of strong winds, but the only report of damage received was out of Lawrence County.
episodes.214292: A frontal boundary initially stalled south of the area, slowly drifted northward into the central Midlands through the day as the northwest flow pattern the region was in, brought a weak shortwave in during the late afternoon. Strong instability and deep mixing brought DCAPE values near 1000 J/kg and an isolated severe storm brought tree damage in Richland, Calhoun, and Orangeburg Counties. Richland County EM also reported a member of the public was injured by a lightning strike.
episodes.214312: A quick-moving mesoscale convective system (MCS) moved southward through parts of Central Alabama during the morning of July 27. Although many trees were downed by sub-severe outflow winds, a couple storms within the MCS did intensify and produce more concentrated areas of tree damage, most notably in southwestern St. Clair County.
episodes.214385: Weak surface low pressure, and a surface trough out ahead of it, produced heavy rain and subsequent flash flooding across portions of New Jersey and Maryland.
episodes.214386: Weak surface low pressure, and a surface trough out ahead of it, produced heavy rain and subsequent flash flooding across portions of New Jersey and Maryland.
episodes.214447: A southward moving cold front produced a cluster of thunderstorms over the area during the afternoon hours. One such storm became severe and produced sporadic wind damage.
episodes.214639: A warm front lifting northward interacted with a surface trough and an unstable airmass to result in widely scattered severe thunderstorms during the evening hours.
episodes.214777: Thunderstorms developed in a warm and humid summer airmass. Some storms produced damaging winds.
episodes.214787: A cluster of thunderstorms developed over western Lake Superior during the early morning hours on Monday (7/27) and tracked southeast just north of a warm front through north-central, northeast, and east-central Wisconsin through the morning and into the early afternoon. The strongest storms produced very large hail up to grapefruit size, damaging straight line winds, and an EF3 tornado in the Appleton and Menasha areas. ||An NWS Storm Survey confirmed a tornado formed around 11:56 AM CDT on the west side of Appleton in Outagamie County and tracked south into northeast Winnebago County, producing EF3 damage in Menasha before moving over Lake Winnebago and dissipating around 12:22 PM CDT. The tornado caused over $100 million in estimated damage, destroyed 85 buildings, produced major damage to 418 buildings, with 1,862 buildings reporting minor damage or affected by the tornado. There were 98 injuries attributed to the tornado (42 direct and 56 indirect).
episodes.214801: Scattered thunderstorms produced very large hail over the Lake Michigan waters during the morning on Monday (7/27).
episodes.214824: Hot summer weather prevailed at the end of July with scattered afternoon and evening storms, some of which were severe.  In addition, extreme heat prevailed on July 28-29 with peak heat index values of 113F or higher.
episodes.214949: Typical summer weather prevailed with scattered afternoon and evening storms, some of which were severe.
episodes.214954: Multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms produced several wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.215254: Multiple supercell thunderstorms moved from north to south across northeast Illinois from the late morning through the early evening of July 27th. Widespread and extensive wind damage occurred in many areas. Large hail occurred in many areas. A total of seven tornadoes occurred. Flooding was reported in numerous areas. At the peak of the storms, at least 500,000 customers were without power in northeast Illinois.
episodes.215255: Scattered supercell thunderstorms moved across northwest Indiana from late morning through early evening on July 27th producing wind damage and one tornado.
episodes.215256: Scattered supercell thunderstorms moved north to south across parts of southern Lake Michigan from the late morning through the afternoon of July 27th, producing severe winds, high waves and a seiche.
episodes.215453: Thunderstorms developed across the region ahead of an approaching warm front.
episodes.215530: In the afternoon of July 27, severe thunderstorms over northeast Illinois continued to strengthen. A bow echo developed and produced instances of damaging winds from far northwest Indiana through east-central Indiana. Damage in northern Indiana consisted primarily of trees and powerlines down, though a couple instances of property damage were noted. One tornado occurred in Grant County, IN.
episodes.215776: A southward moving cold front brought scattered showers and thunderstorms to portions of the inland rivers during the afternoon hours of July twenty-seventh. With ample instability and wind shear in place a few of the storms became severe in nature bringing strong wind gusts to portions of the Pamlico and Neuse Rivers.
episodes.215777: Clusters of thunderstorms developed along a warm front across east-central and southeast Illinois during the early morning of July 27th.  While most of the storms were sub-severe, one cell produced a wet microburst with estimated wind gusts of 80-90mph near Effingham.  Other storms caused pockets of flooding and minor wind damage near Mattoon in Coles County.
episodes.215853: A strong storm moved southeastward over Silver Bay during the early evening of the 26th. The Silver Bay GLOS station had just been returned to service and recorded strong winds from this storm with gusts to 69 mph. A heat burst also occurred with this storm at Silver Bay.
episodes.215854: On July 26, 2026, a intense heat dome surged across northeastern Minnesota, bringing dangerous tropical-like humidity and uncharacteristically oppressive heat to northeastern Minnesota. Driven by dew points pushing into the mid-to-upper 70s, the heat prompted the issuance of Heat Advisories and Extreme Heat Warnings across the area. The event saw peak heat index values frequently reach 95��F to 105��F across the Northland. Some of the highest heat index readings recorded across the NWS Duluth coverage area included: Brainerd: 105��F, Pine City: 104��F, Aitkin & Grand Rapids: 103��F, Grand Marais: 102��F, Duluth (Airport / Downtown): 98��F���100��F, Hibbing & International Falls: 96��F���98��F, with a few personal weather stations reaching higher into the 110��F���115��F range. |Beyond the sheer heat index numbers, the event was notable for how uncommon such high dew points are for the region, where Lake Superior normally moderates summer extremes. The extreme humidity suppressed nighttime cooling, keeping overnight lows near 70��F across much of the area. |As a front approached that evening, the extreme heat and moisture triggered severe thunderstorms across parts of northeastern Minnesota. The strongest storms tracked across northern St. Louis and Lake counties into the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness and the Iron Range, producing intense cloud-to-ground lightning, localized heavy downpours, and severe hail���including reports of quarter- to ping-pong-ball-sized hail near Cook and Tower.
episodes.215855: A tropical-like air mass that impacted northwest Wisconsin on July 26, 2026, prompting the issuance of Heat Advisories and Extreme Heat Warnings. Driven by unseasonably high dew points surging into the mid-to-upper 70s and air temperatures climbing into the low-to-mid 90s, peak heat index values reached stifling levels across the region. Peak readings soared to 104��F in Spooner and Shell Lake, 102��F in Hayward and Rice Lake, 101��F to 103��F in Superior and Solon Springs, 100��F to 101��F in Ashland, and up to 100��F in Price County locations like Phillips and Park Falls.||The event was particularly notable because strong southerly winds held typical Lake Superior breezes at bay, allowing oppressive heat to push directly to the shoreline in communities like Superior and Ashland that normally receive coastal cooling. Furthermore, the extreme atmospheric moisture prevented nighttime cooling, keeping overnight lows between 70��F and 74��F across much of northwest Wisconsin and denying non-air-conditioned homes relief. ||As a front pushed into this volatile, energy-rich air mass late that evening and into the early morning hours of July 27, a severe thunderstorm complex erupted across northern Minnesota. Moving rapidly out of northeastern Minnesota into Bayfield and Ashland counties, storms produced hail to the size of baseballs near Port Wing.
episodes.215863: Clusters of thunderstorms developed along the northeastern periphery of a strong upper-level ridge centered over the Central Plains during the afternoon of July 27th.  The convection formed across Wisconsin into northeastern Illinois, then dropped southeastward into north-central Indiana.  One of the storm clusters grazed Vermilion County where storm spotters observed a brief tornado touchdown west of Hoopeston.  Additional cells developed along an outflow boundary as far west as Shelbyville, then dropped southeastward across the I-70 corridor during the evening.  Some of the storms produced 70-80mph wind gusts and significant tree and crop damage across portions of Clark and Crawford counties.
episodes.215909: Multiple rounds of thunderstorms impacted the coast and the adjacent coastal waters throughout the day. The first round developed in the late morning hours in the Charleston area and produced strong wind gusts in Charleston Harbor. Another round developed in the late evening hours and produced strong wind gusts across the Atlantic coastal waters adjacent to Beaufort County.
episodes.215912: A large cluster of thunderstorms developed across Beaufort County in the evening hours. The storm produced several instances of damaging wind gusts across Beaufort.
episodes.215950: A cool front slowly shifted southward through Georgia on July 25th before stalling and diffusing across southeastern Georgia by July 26th. Pre-frontal showers and storms moved through from northwest to southeast in the afternoon and evening of July 25th. Higher moisture and slow steering flow allowed for heavy downpours and training storms in flood-prone areas. Lower moisture and increasing subsidence aloft limited storm coverage on July 26th. Another stronger cold front moved southward across Georgia July 27th into 28th before stalling over southeast Georgia on July 29th. On July 27th, some shortwaves aloft moved through north central FL enhancing sea breeze thunderstorms. On July 29th, extreme heat, high moisture, and high mixed level CAPE ahead of the front helped develop strong to severe storms across southeast Georgia and northeast Florida.
episodes.216083: Isolated thunderstorms developed over Chase County during the early afternoon hours of July 27th. Storms became severe and tracked to the east into Hayes and southern Lincoln County. Hail up to the size of golf balls was reported near Enders and a thunderstorm wind gust of 67 MPH was reported near Dickens.
episodes.216110: A prolific monsoon pattern continued to end July, resulting in additional instances of thunderstorm wind gusts and flash flooding. Additionally, an active wildfire resulted in the development of a brief fire tornado.
episodes.216422: A cluster of storm moving in from the west produced high wind in central and north central South Dakota, with a 68 mph gust recorded on the South Dakota State University mesonet station 6 miles north northwest of Lantry (Dewey County) and a 60 mph wind gust was estimated by the public 7 miles south southwest of Capa in Jones county.
episodes.216618: During the late afternoon hours on the 27th, a slow-moving cluster of thunderstorms developed over portions of east-central and northeast Colorado. A 61 mph wind gust was measured in Yuma County.
episodes.216642: From the afternoon through the late evening hours on the 27th, a few clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms moved east to southeast across portions of southwest Nebraska. A wind gust up to 68 mph was measured in Red Willow County.
episodes.216648: One severe thunderstorm developed with orographic ascent along the Pennsylvania ridges in an environment with around 1000 J/kg of MLCAPE and DCAPE of 900 J/kg. A strong downburst resulted and produced notable tree damage.
episodes.216814: An upper-level trough and an associated surface feature initiated a few supercells in the Piedmont region of central Virginia late in the evening on July 26. These supercells tracked south to southeast and produced a swath of significant damaging wind and hail in some locations. These storms persisted into the early morning hours of July 27, before moving south of the area.
episodes.216815: During the late afternoon and evening hours on the 27th, a few clusters of thunderstorms moved east to northeast across portions of northwest Kansas. The strongest activity produced estimated 80 to 100 mph winds in Cheyenne and Thomas Counties. These severe winds produced sporadic hefty damage, including a blown apart garage, grain bins swept off their foundations, trees snapped, and a tipped over semi.
episodes.216855: Isolated to scattered thunderstorms developed as instability increased. The available instability was enough to support a few stronger storms with isolated damaging wind gusts, but overall instability remained limited, keeping the severe weather threat low.
episodes.216961: Storms brought large swaths of severe and damaging wind gusts that caused some damage and blow overs long interstate 90.
episodes.216968: A line of thunderstorms moved across eastern Wyoming and brought some strong wind gusts, mainly to Campbell county with lesser gusts in Crook and Weston counties.
episodes.217005: Over much of the end of July, including on July 26th and 27th, a persistent northwest flow mid- and upper-level pattern set up from the Great Lakes down into the Tennessee Valley. This allowed a series of mesoscale convective systems to drop from north to south across the region, each of which brought strong to severe thunderstorms with swaths of damaging winds to the Ohio Valley. On July 26th, a cluster of storms initiated over southwest Indiana and southern Illinois during the afternoon hours before pushing to the south-southeast into western and south central Kentucky. While the most potent portion of this complex impacted areas just to the west of the NWS Louisville warning area, a few instances of wind damage were observed as the complex of storms moved across the Cave region of south central Kentucky. On July 27th, the pattern shifted to the north and east across the region, bringing the main storm track into southeast Indiana and the Bluegrass region of Kentucky. An MCS descending from central Indiana would produce scattered wind damage as it moved across the area, with a smattering of tree damage and a few wind gusts exceeding 60 mph observed.
episodes.217040: A strong upper high was centered over New Mexico, but residual mid level moisture contributed to high based thunderstorms with damaging winds as temperatures reached 100-105 degrees.
episodes.217087: An isolated storm developed along a sea breeze boundary in far southeast Virginia on the afternoon of July 27. There were a few reports of wind damage in southern portions of the City of Virginia Beach.
episodes.217088: A warm and unstable airmass with weak surface allowed slow-moving storms to develop in the late morning and early afternoon of July 27. Heavy rainfall associated with these storms allowed for a few instances of flash flooding across eastern Virginia in the afternoon hours.
episodes.217089: A nearly stationary, isolated storm develop in the urban Richmond metro corridor during the late afternoon on July 26. Isolated flash flooding was observed in this area before the storm moved south and dissipated later that evening. A separate storm moved through in the early morning of July 27 with some flooding reports again in the Richmond metro region.
episodes.217176: A cold front associated with low pressure moving through Manitoba combined with a very moist and unstable airmass to trigger strong to severe thunderstorms over the U.P.
episodes.217177: A cold front associated with low pressure moving through Manitoba combined with a very moist and unstable airmass to trigger strong to severe thunderstorms over the U.P.
episodes.217190: Low pressure, a warm front and unstable conditions led to numerous thunderstorms over east central and southeast WI. Large hail and damaging winds occurred.
episodes.217202: During the afternoon of July 27th, a cluster of thunderstorms swept through the St. Louis metropolitan area. In Madison County, severe winds snapped a few large trees near Lewis and Clark Community College.
episodes.217230: A complex of thunderstorms dove south from Kentucky into Middle Tennessee during the evening hours of July 26, 2026, scraping the Tennessee River Valley along the way. Substantial instability with SBCAPEs over 4500 J/kg combined with bulk shear values of 30 knots supported a few severe storms with isolated wind damage in Decatur County.
episodes.217233: A warm and humid air mass was in place on July 27 allowing scattered thunderstorm development, primarily along ridgelines and sea breezes.
episodes.217234: A warm and humid air mass was in place on July 27 allowing scattered thunderstorm development, primarily along ridgelines and sea breezes.
episodes.217336: Strong thunderstorms developed over Lake Superior and tracked southeastward into the eastern UP during the overnight into the early morning on the 27th, producing large hail across parts of the Eastern Upper Peninsula of Michigan.
episodes.217337: Following early morning storms across the eastern UP, additional storms developed across northeast Lower Michigan during the late morning into the early afternoon hours, producing heavy rain and some localized hail near the town of Oscoda, MI.

A brief tornado with estimated peak winds of 75 mph touched down southwest of the intersection of Stacy Court and Railroad Street. This tornado moved generally southward causing mainly tree and power line damage along its path. A few homes and one car were damaged. The tornado ended near the intersection of Hawthorne Boulevard and Park Boulevard.

A brief tornado with estimated peak winds of 80 mph touched down near Liberty Drive just west of Hillside Court. A concentrated corridor of damage occurred in the vicinity of Indiana Street and Campbell Avenue along Pershing Avenue where the tops of several softwood trees were snapped and numerous tree limbs were blown down. The tornado continued moving southward producing sporadic tree damage until it ended near Alchester Drive and Wales Drive.

An NWS Damage Survey team confirmed a tornado touched down around 11:56 AM CDT in Appleton in urban southern Outagamie County. The tornado developed just north of Wisconsin Avenue, partially tearing the roof off houses and several businesses on Wisconsin Avenue consistent with EF0 damage and winds of 85 mph. The tornado strengthened south of Wisconsin Avenue to EF1 by collapsing exterior walls to a warehouse building east of North Perkins Street with winds of 110 mph. The tornado continued producing EF1 damage to warehouses, retail buildings and strip malls as it continued south to College Avenue. The tornado strengthened to EF2 south of College Avenue near South Perkins Street by buckling the roof purlins to a metal building structure with winds of 118 mph. The tornado continued to produce EF1 damage through the rest of southern Outagamie County, by snapping and uprooting trees as well as causing damage to residential buildings. The tornado reached the county line around 12:00 PM CDT as it crossed the Fox River while widening to around 1000 yards. The tornado then crossed into Winnebago County, where it would eventually reach EF3 intensity.

An NWS Damage Survey team confirmed a tornado that originated in Outagamie County around 11:56 AM CDT continued moving south, entering northeastern Winnebago County around 12:00 PM CDT. The tornado produced EF1 damage by snapping and uprooting trees and damaging residential buildings just south of the Fox River. The tornado continued to widen and eventually strengthened again to EF2 damage just south of Palisades Drive by uplifting significant portions of the roof deck and collapsing garage doors to residences with winds of 120 mph. The tornado continued to strengthen and widen, reaching a width of 1400 yards and producing EF3 damage to a well-built low-rise brick building just north of Highway 10 in Menasha. At this location, significant damage occurred to the exterior walls and some interior walls with winds of 140 mph.||The tornado path then narrowed south of Highway 10 in Menasha to just below 1000 yards, producing pockets of EF2 damage along and just south of Midway Road by collapsing an entire roof with winds of 125 mph. EF2 damage was also observed east of Highway 10 near Airport Road with the collapse of the exterior walls of a small professional building and winds of 135 mph. The tornado continued south and damaged the bleachers at Calder Stadium east of Racine Road, consistent with EF2 damage and winds of 120 mph.||The tornado widened again as it tracked south, reaching its maximum width of 1500 yards between 5th and 6th street in Menasha between Little Lake Butte des Morts and northern Lake Winnebago. The tornado again reached EF3 intensity just south of this area, between Plank Road and 3rd Street. In this area a car was flipped over, there was a collapse of exterior walls of a small retail building, and a house was destroyed with winds of 140 mph.||The tornado continued south, crossing the Menasha Channel and producing EF2 damage to eastern Doty Island east of Smith Park with large sections of roof structures removed to residential structures along with snapped trees and exterior walls collapsed on one residence with winds of 130 mph. The tornado then tracked over Lake Winnebago passing east of Neenah Point. Although the tornado at this point mainly stayed over the water, it did clip Davis Point, producing EF0 damage by uprooting trees with winds of 85 mph. The tornado continued south and eventually dissipated over Lake Winnebago somewhere east of Perkins Point around 12:22 PM CDT.

The tornado produced tree damage and cosmetic structure damage as it moved north. The tornado turned northwest after crossing 159th Street and reached its northernmost point between 155th Street and 154th Street. The tornado turned back to the south and accelerated as it crossed 159th Street again. The tornado was likely at peak intensity as it removed a roof from an industrial building on 167th Street and caused exterior roof and wall damage to an apartment complex on 171st Street. Ground and drone surveys found a swath of sporadic wind damage|from Sweetser to Marion and near Gas City Indiana. Within this|swath, evidence of a weak, disorganized circulation touching down|was noted in some locations. The tornadic damage began in a|cornfield near W 200 N and N 500 W on the north side of Sweetser,|IN. The tornado crossed over the cornfield and impacted a|neighborhood on the northeast side of Sweetser. Several large|tree branches were downed and a few tree trunks snapped on Allen|Drive, Mary Lou Road, and Laura Lane. The tornado continued|southeast, affecting residences on W Magers Road where|significant tree damage occurred including a large tree falling|on the roof of a house. Another residence experienced large tree|branches downed along with damage to fencing. The tornado crossed|N 400 and caused damage to an apartment complex including large|tree branches downed and some roof damage to a few of the|apartment buildings. The tornado then affected open fields before|crossing State Road 18 causing damage to a trucking company|facility on the south side of State Road 18. Much of the roofing|material was removed, but the plywood boards remained intact.|Some of the debris from the damage to this facility was tossed to|the north side of State Road 18 including a steel reel. The|tornado then continued southeast across open fields between|County Roads 325W and 200W before causing extensive tree damage|to residences from W 9th Street to W 16th Street between Buffalo|Avenue and Norton Avenue. Survey results indicate a transition|occurred from tornado damage to straight line wind damage on the|south side of Marion to the southeast of State Road 9 and towards|Gas City. Maximum winds are estimated around 75 mph.
